content: 1. The incidence of cervical cancer in Eastern Africa is estimated at 350 cases per 100,000 women. Among these, 2% of women are diagnosed with CIN 2+ (Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia grade 2 or higher), equating to approximately 20,000 women. Of these, 30% experience regression, leaving 14,000 women with persistent CIN 2+. 2. In the model calculations, it is assumed that there is no cervical cancer in true negatives (TN) or false positives (FP). Additionally, no CIN 2+ is assumed in TN or FP cases. 3. For false negatives (FN), the model assumes a 90% persistence rate of CIN 2+ without treatment, with a 10% regression rate. For cases treated with cold knife conization (CKC), the regression rate is 2%. 4. Major bleeding is assumed to be absent in TN and FN cases, as these individuals are not treated. However, 0.001705 of the population treated with CKC is expected to experience major bleeding, based on pooled data from observational studies. 5. The risk of premature delivery is estimated at 5% in the general population, with 0.001705 of women treated with CKC expected to experience premature delivery. 6. No data were identified regarding the risk of infertility following treatment for CIN 2+. 7. Major infections are assumed to be absent in TN and FN cases, as these individuals are not treated. However, 0.000888 of the population treated with CKC is expected to develop major infections. 8. Minor infections are also assumed to be absent in TN and FN cases. However, 0.009368 of the population treated with CKC is expected to develop minor infections. 9. The number of cancers detected during first-time screening was calculated based on data from Sankaranarayanan et al. (2005). For single screening tests, the number of screen-detected cancers was determined for women participating in the screening program. For tests involving colposcopy, the number of cancers detected included both screen-detected and clinically detected cases. 10. In the no screen group, no cancers would be detected. This does not represent the annual incidence of cervical cancer but rather the prevalence of cancer at the time of initial screening. 11. The expert panel recommends a screen-and-treat strategy using visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) followed by cryotherapy (or LEEP if cryotherapy is not suitable) over cytology followed by colposcopy (with or without biopsy) and treatment with cryotherapy or LEEP. This recommendation is based on fewer harms associated with VIA, despite some overtreatment and fewer cancers detected at first-time screening. VIA requires fewer resources compared to cytology programs, which involve additional training, quality control, and follow-up visits. 12. The diagnostic accuracy of VIA compared to cytology followed by colposcopy was assessed. VIA has a pooled sensitivity of 77% and specificity of 82%, while cytology (ASCUS threshold) has a pooled sensitivity of 84% and specificity of 88%. Colposcopic impression has a pooled sensitivity of 95% but a lower specificity of 42%. The overall quality of evidence for these outcomes is low due to limitations in study design, indirectness, and imprecision. 13. The mortality from cervical cancer in HIV-positive women was assumed to be the same as in women of unknown HIV status, with 250 deaths per 350 women diagnosed with cervical cancer. 14. The resource implications of VIA are lower compared to cytology programs, which require additional training, quality control, and follow-up visits. Colposcopy following cytology also necessitates a second visit. 15. The evidence for VIA compared to cytology followed by colposcopy in screening for CIN 2+ in HIV-positive women is based on pooled sensitivity and specificity data. VIA has a sensitivity of 77% and specificity of 83%, while cytology followed by colposcopy has a sensitivity of 84% and specificity of 88%. The quality of evidence for these outcomes is low due to variability in study results and limitations in study design. 16. The outcomes of different screening and treatment strategies were compared, including mortality from cervical cancer, incidence of cervical cancer, recurrence of CIN 2+, major bleeding, premature delivery, major infections, minor infections, and unnecessary treatment. VIA-based strategies generally require fewer resources but may result in slightly higher rates of overtreatment and fewer cancers detected at first-time screening compared to cytology-based strategies. This summary reflects the detailed findings and assumptions made in the analysis of cervical cancer screening and treatment strategies.
